Well...this video is obviously intended for a particular audience. His arguments depend on the viewer accepting certain intuitions - that modern art is aesthetically lacking relative to classical art, for example. Given that premise and the others he clearly expects the viewer to intuit themselves, I think he offers some fairly convincing arguments.

His exercise with the Jackson Pollock painting vs. his studio apron splattered with random paint differs from your classical art alternative in an important way: if you were to offer graduate students in art classical art piece that was bunk, they would actually analyze it as bunk (e.g. they may assume it was an early study, to explain flawed work from a great master). You'd have to produce a fair imitation to pull one over on students of classical art, which would model the objective standards of aesthetics and artistic excellence he was talking about.

I saw the point of that exercise as a way of demonstrating that classical art has clear, objective standards by which it can be judged, which Jackson Pollock paintings may lack.

One could resist this conclusion by arguing that the Jackson Pollock paintings do embody standards by which they can be judged, but which aren't being taught in university because they are poorly understood by the art establishment, for example. But I don't believe it should be dismissed as absurd on its face - he had a point there, whose truth or falsity isn't trivial.

I pretty much agree with much of his assessment regarding modern art, but reject the assumption that this is all bad. It really does seem that aesthetic appreciation has been largely abandoned in much of modern art in favor of personal expression. I feel this demands a new language for talking about these works, which perhaps should not be called art. They certainly aren't art in the same sense that classical realist paintings are art.

But it seems to me that they aren't art in the way that Rothko or Pollock are, either. Because to me, there is obvious aesthetic appeal to these modern artists. It isn't the same as classical art, but there is some commonality. They are certainly both beautiful to me.

Because of this, I rejected many conclusions from the video. But I did feel it was a reasonable and thoughtful analysis, and I certainly recognized his conclusions as generally following from his arguments. I just don't share his intuition that all the modern art he discussed lacks aesthetic beauty and mastery.

Don't get me wrong. I mostly agree with him, but he's missing some major points.

1) Painting used to have more practical applications leading to a more robust talent pool.

Back in the day, where paintings like the ones he reveres were made, paintings were mainstream contemporary media. If you wanted a picture of your mother to cherish after she died, you'd have to get a painting commissioned. If you wanted a sign for your store, you'd have to hire an actual painter to paint it. Being a painter was a day job for a lot of people, and rising to the top of this industry, the supremely talented were commissioned by the wealthy to create works of art as both symbols of status and as attractions. That's where those master works came from: the best of the best of a large pool of professional artistic painters. For example, we still have archery today, but the best archers to have ever lived were probably from an era in which archery were a common part of everyday life.

These days, new forms of media have replaced painting for the majority of utilitarian purposes. Photography has replaced painting for portraiture, graphic design software has largely replaced painting for signage, and movies, games, and web media, have largely replaced painting as a form of visual spectical. So, while society has expanded, the painting indusrty has comparatively dwindled. This has the additional effect of luring many of today's most talented artists away from painting and into new art forms, and many of those making movies, games and graphic advertisement would likley have been painters in times passed. Where, in times past, the best engineer in your town may've been a blacksmith or a mason, blacksmithing no longer attracts much of today's top engineering talent. Similarly, few of today's top artists are compelled to pursue a career in painting.

This all contributes to a situation where modern painters, even if they were trying, would have a tough time going toe to toe with the ancient masters in terms of sheer technical proficiency, but the most important component is probably that of a changing market.

2) With utilitarian purposes gone, the primary remaining market for art is as a symbol of wealth.

If a modern artist could make something akin to the Sistine chapel, they'd probably still do quite well for themselves, but few modern artists can approach that level of mastery. For a contemporary artist, they're much more likley to be able to gain notariety through being controversial than by being talented. If you're rich, looking for a way to display your status, you're better off buying a painting that's provocative and famous than by buying some artists mediocre imitation of rennesance-era techniques.

There's still plenty of amazing art made these days, maybe the best ever: http://www.cgsociety.org/gallery/home/like-count/desc.

It's just not done on canvas. So, while I agree with his overall point about the inanity of modern painting scene, it's not art that is dieing, only painting itself. In the same way horseback riding and archery have lost their mainstream purpose, so too is painting drifting into the realm of excentric hobby for the enthusiast.

This is (somewhat) objectively measurable, and something that takes a lot of time and effort to learn. On the other hand, there's beauty, or interestingness, or some other -thing- that incites feelings in whoever looks upon the piece of art. This is, if at all, immensely more difficult to measure and relies on the creativity and inventiveness of the creator. These are not skills, they are talents: they can be honed, but not everyone is capable of acquiring them.

In any case, I don't fully disagree with the video, but I do thing it oversimplifies things a bit if its conclusion is that the only "good" art is the technically hard art. Because that's ignoring a whole aspect of it, which is at least as important.

Historically, changes in art have resulted in people decrying 'new art' as horrible.

The situation is similar to music.

He's speaking from the standpoint of a classical art professor, so he's bound to think what's so different now isn't as good, but he doesn't take into account the fact that there is now a vastly different audience from when the great masters were active. Art is more accessible now. Instead of having to commission one of the masters, or know someone who could afford to do so, you can see it on the internet. Materials are less expensive. You don't have to mix paint from stuff you find in the woods, or use it before the egg yolks dry out. You can literally go to a hardware store and buy spray paint, and you're done. That exposure also brings new critics. Everyone's a critic, and everyone can see it, so instead of being a fine art critic, you need absolutely no background in art to be able to judge art.

He does sort of have a point to a certain extent, regarding the modern art that is literally just something the "artist" found, and defined as art. A giant rock isn't art. It's a rock. Saying it's art is one of the reasons there's such a backlash against "all modern art". Yeah, there's a LOT of really cool stuff that this guy glazes over when he says modern art is bad, but it's a blanket statement, so he's also covering a lot of bullshit art.

You don't really see many modern masters. Sure, there are Norman Rockwells, but come to think of it, most of the more successful "modern artists" who come up with truly well-crafted art now work for marketing companies, design games (I don't care who tells us otherwise, some games are most definitely art), or have found some other way to monetize their art. At the same time, not many of the shitty Renaissance and pre-Renaissance artists are famous. All you need to do is walk through the Vatican Museum to see where a lot of the terrible art from the same time frame as the great masters is kept. Almost every painting is religious in nature, and it was able to be produced because the Church was one of the only groups that had the free time and resources to produce "art".

This guy also glazes over some of the most well-known artists, probably because he doesn't consider their form of art "art". The amount of thought, the style, and the messages that Banksy comes up with will probably last for as long as the great masters' work.

Part of the problem of judging art nowadays is that there are so many more forms of art than were accessible during the Renaissance. In his video, this guy mentions two forms: paintings (albeit several types of paint), and sculpture (rock carving in particular). Now we have video (films are totally art, animation is totally art), photography, writing (journalism, fiction, nonfiction), performance art (now mainstream because of accessibility and because we have the ability to record and preserve performances), game design, music that doesn't need to be performed by different orchestras from sheets, and probably thousands of other types. There is no metric to judge each one of them, and no standard to compare them to.

Then there's the "I put this here, so it's art now" movement that exploded after Marcel DuChamp's urinal "art". The stuff you can look at and say "oh, COME ON". The white triptych in the background at the end is a perfect example of that. It's the endless enablement of "artists" who put almost no effort into coming up with the "art", and all of the trouble into explaining why it's art.

Maybe he's just bitter that he goes to so much trouble to make his form of art, and knows that the great masters did too, and resents the fact that some modern artists just explain away their lack of effort, and thrive on it. Maybe he thinks that art should be visually painstakingly precise. If Jackson Pollock can use splatter painting to make something that's visually appealing, yeah, sure, that's art. It performs all of the functions that art needs to, but at the end of the day, he absolutely did not go to nearly the same trouble as the great masters to produce. It's the difference between Hans Zimmer's soundtracks and the Canadian rapper, Chuggo. Are they both music? Yes. Do they both have audiences that would loathe the other? Yes. Is one more worthy than the other as definitively "music"? Absolutely. There are the great masters who practice for years. The kid from Whiplash who fights like hell to nail every note in perfect time, and he's up against American Idol contestants who are massively successful, but have never put much of any effort into it, and only work because they make boatloads of money and have forced exposure. If I went to the amount of trouble that this professor went to, or knew how much trouble his peers went to, only to see them become baristas to pay the rent, I'd be pissed too.

This guy's arguments sound pretty much like the dude sitting out on his lawn grumping about "Kids these days." I might even agree that, yeah, some contemporary art is dogshit but, come on... "with each successive generation the standards have decreased until there are no standards??" Fuck that. This guy has his head up his ass. There are more talented artists putting out amazingly good work today than there ever has been.

And movements in art change because artists are tired of rehashing the same shit. And shock art is successful because dipshits like this guy are shocked and offended by it. It's about innovation and creativity... sometimes there are hits, sometimes there are misses but you see the misses in art history books because it's important to acknowledge that someone tried something new. And Fuck it, The Madonna with elephant dung, Piss Christ, etc. have done more to galvanize our sense of freedom of speech and pull the teeth out of the concept of "blasphemy" than this guy's shit ever will.

Also... What graduate student in art would ever think that was a Jackson Pollock??
